title: Given a string of digits 2–9, return all letter combinations the number could spell, based on the classic phone keypad mapping.
shortTitle: Letter Combinations of a Phone Number

s1_definition.profdef: Map each digit to its keypad letters and backtrack across the digit positions: at depth d, append each letter of digit d and recurse to depth d+1, recording a combination when the path length equals the number of digits. The result size is the product of the per-digit letter counts.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India lets customers create a vanity reference by typing digits that map to letters on a keypad, like old phone spelling. For each digit you try each of its letters, moving to the next digit, until you've spelled a full word-length combination.
s1_definition.oneliner: For each digit append each of its letters and recurse to the next digit; record when all digits are consumed.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Map each digit to its keypad letters and backtrack across the digit positions: at depth d, append each letter of digit d and recurse to depth d+1, recording a combination when the path length equals the number of digits. The result size is the product of the per-digit letter counts.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** National Bank of India lets customers create a vanity reference by typing digits that map to letters on a keypad, like old phone spelling. For each digit you try each of its letters, moving to the next digit, until you've spelled a full word-length combination.

**One line to remember:** For each digit append each of its letters and recurse to the next digit; record when all digits are consumed.

sections.s2_technical:
Store a digit-to-letters map (2 maps to "abc", and so on). Backtrack with an index into the digit string and a StringBuilder path. When the index equals the string length, record the path; otherwise loop over the current digit's letters, append one, recurse with index+1, and remove it. For example: `for (char c : map.get(digit)) { sb.append(c); backtrack(index+1); sb.deleteCharAt(sb.length()-1); }`.

An empty input must return an empty list, not a list containing an empty string, so guard that case. The time is O(4^n · n) in the worst case, since digits seven and nine have four letters each.

A senior nuance is that an iterative queue-based expansion produces the same result without recursion, which can be cleaner when the digit count is large and stack depth is a concern.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, a customer picks a memorable vanity code for a payee by entering keypad digits, and the UI must suggest every letter combination those digits can spell. This is exactly how Letter Combinations works.

Problem 2 — Every combination must span all entered digits exactly once, in order. This is exactly why the backtracking advances one digit per recursion level and records only at full depth.

The mini-project builds a `VanityCodeSuggester`, a `BankLogFormatter`, and a runnable demo.

sections.s5_journey:
The input digits are two and three.

Step 1: Digit two maps to a, b, c; digit three maps to d, e, f.

Step 2: Choosing a then d, e, f yields ad, ae, af.

Step 3: Choosing b then d, e, f yields bd, be, bf.

Step 4: Choosing c then d, e, f yields cd, ce, cf.

Step 5: Nine combinations, the product of three letters times three letters.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Letter Combinations of a Phone Number is a product-space backtracking over the digit positions. I keep a map from each digit to its keypad letters, then recurse with an index into the digit string and a string builder holding the current partial spelling. When the index reaches the end of the digit string I record the completed combination; otherwise I loop over the current digit's letters, append one, recurse to the next digit, and remove it to backtrack.

The one edge case that trips people up is empty input, which must return an empty list rather than a list containing an empty string, so I guard it explicitly. The worst-case cost is about four to the n times n, because digits seven and nine each contribute four letters.

In my project at National Bank of India, customers chose a memorable vanity code for a payee by typing keypad digits, and the interface suggested every letter combination those digits could spell. This backtracking generated the suggestions in order, and when the digit count grew I noted that an iterative queue-based expansion gives the same result without deep recursion.
